'''Robert Arthur Oberlender''' (born July 25, 1956) is an [[American people|American]] [[medicinal chemist]] known for his work in the areas of [[serotonergic drug|serotonergic]] and [[dopaminergic]] [[drug]]s as well as [[drug discrimination]].<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation">{{cite web | title=Robert A. Oberlender, PhD | website=The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson's Research | url=https://www.michaeljfox.org/researcher/robert-oberlender-phd | access-date=16 June 2025}}</ref><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021">{{cite podcast | url=https://www.patreon.com/posts/podcast-26-with-55228463 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220819000000/https://www.patreon.com/posts/podcast-26-with-55228463 | archive-date=19 August 2022 | title=PODCAST 26: An interview with Vyvanse inventor Dr. Robert Oberlender | website=[[Hamilton Morris#Podcast|The Hamilton Morris Podcast]] | publisher=Patreon | host=[[Hamilton Morris]] | date=22 August 2021}} [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x9WmEVRxebE Alt URL]</ref><ref name="Oberlender1989" /> He is most well known for his discovery and development of [[lisdexamfetamine]] (lysine–dextroamphetamine), which is now marketed as a [[pharmaceutical drug]] under the brand name Vyvanse and is prescribed as a misuse-resistant [[stimulant]] in the treatment of [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] (ADHD) and other conditions.<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /><ref name="RonceroÁlvarez2014">{{cite journal | vauthors = Roncero C, Álvarez FJ | title = The use of lisdexamfetamine dimesylate for the treatment of ADHD and other psychiatric disorders | journal = Expert Rev Neurother | volume = 14 | issue = 8 | pages = 849–865 | date = August 2014 | pmid = 24948428 | doi = 10.1586/14737175.2014.932691 | url = }}</ref>

== Biography ==

Oberlender attended the pharmacy school of [[Temple University]] in his hometown of [[Philadelphia, Pennsylvania]], receiving a [[bachelor's degree]], and worked for two years as a [[pharmacist]].<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="Oberlender1989" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> Then, he started a [[Ph.D.]] program in medicinal chemistry at [[Purdue University]] in 1981.<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /><ref name="Oberlender1989" /> He worked in the lab of [[psychedelic drug|psychedelic]] [[chemist]] [[David E. Nichols]] studying psychedelics, [[entactogen]]s, and related drugs, first completing his Ph.D. and then continuing in the lab as a [[postdoc]].<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /><ref name="Oberlender1989" /> His first publication with the lab was in 1984<ref name="OberlenderKothariNichols1984">{{cite journal | vauthors = Oberlender RA, Kothari PJ, Nichols DE, Zabik JE | title = Substituent branching in phenethylamine-type hallucinogens: a comparison of 1-[2,5-dimethoxy-4-(2-butyl)phenyl]-2-aminopropane and 1-[2,5-dimethoxy-4-(2-methylpropyl)phenyl]-2-aminopropane | journal = J Med Chem | volume = 27 | issue = 6 | pages = 788–792 | date = June 1984 | pmid = 6737421 | doi = 10.1021/jm00372a015 | url = https://chemistry.mdma.ch/hiveboard/rhodium/pdf/nichols/nichols-branched.4-substituents.pdf}}</ref> and his last publication with the group was in 1995, a period spanning more than 10{{nbsp}}years.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /><ref name="OberlenderRamachandranJohnson1995">{{cite journal | vauthors = Oberlender R, Ramachandran PV, Johnson MP, Huang X, Nichols DE | title = Effect of a chiral 4-alkyl substituent in hallucinogenic amphetamines | journal = J Med Chem | volume = 38 | issue = 18 | pages = 3593–3601 | date = September 1995 | pmid = 7658446 | doi = 10.1021/jm00018a019 | url = }}</ref> His [[Ph.D. thesis]], published in 1989, was on [[stereoselectivity|stereoselective]] actions of psychedelics, including the [[substituted lysergamide|lysergamide]]s [[LA-Aziridine]] and [[LA-3Cl-SB]] and the [[DOx (psychedelics)|DOx]] drugs [[DOIB (drug)|DOIB]] and [[DOSB (drug)|DOSB]], as well as on drug discrimination studies of entactogens, including [[MDA (drug)|MDA]], [[MDMA]], [[MBDB]], and [[MDAI]].<ref name="Oberlender1989">{{cite thesis | last=Oberlender | first=Robert Arthur | title=Stereoselective Aspects of Hallucinogenic Drug Action and Drug Discrimination Studies of Entactogens | date=May 1989 | publisher=[[Purdue University]] | url=https://www.proquest.com/openview/1e352c58f79a5c3e8bf32b98df2f04af/ | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250615000000/https://www.proquest.com/openview/1e352c58f79a5c3e8bf32b98df2f04af/ | archive-date=15 June 2025}} [https://bitnest.netfirms.com/external/Theses/Oberlender1989 Alt URL]</ref><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" />

Oberlender personally [[self-experimentation|self-experimented]] with some of the [[psychoactive drug]]s [[chemical synthesis|synthesized]] in the Nichols lab.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> In the mid-1990s, he tried the obscure psychedelic [[substituted tryptamine|tryptamine]] [[5-MeO-pyr-T]], a [[synthetic compound|synthetic]] [[structural analog|analogue]] of [[5-MeO-DMT]], and accidentally [[overdose|took too high of a dose of it]] without a [[trip sitter]] present.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> While under the influence of 5-MeO-pyr-T, Oberlender stripped naked, began wandering the Purdue University campus in a [[fugue state]], and was apprehended by campus police.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> His case did not end up going to court, but the incident did result in Oberlender having to leave Nichols's lab.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> His [[trip report|experience]] with 5-MeO-pyr-T was subsequently published anonymously in [[Alexander Shulgin]]'s 1997 book ''[[TiHKAL]]'' (''Tryptamines I Have Known and Loved'').<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /><ref name="TiHKAL1997">{{cite book | author1 = [[Alexander T. Shulgin]] | author2 = [[Ann Shulgin]] | chapter = #43. 5-MeO-pyr-T; TRYPTAMINE, 5-METHOXY-N,N-TETRAMETHYLENE; INDOLE, 5-METHOXY-3-[2-(1-PYRROLIDYL)- ETHYL]; PYRROLIDINE, 1-[2-(5-METHOXY-1H-INDOL-3-YL)ETHYL]; 5-METHOXY-N,N-TETRAMETHYLENETRYPTAMINE; 5-METHOXY-3-[2-(1-PYRROLIDYL)ETHYL]INDOLE; 1-[2-(5-METHOXY-1H-INDOL-3-YL)ETHYL]PYRROLIDINE; “PYRROLIDYL-5-METHOXYTRYPTAMINE” | pages = 548–551 | title = TiHKAL: The Continuation | publisher = [[Transform Press]] | date = 1997 | edition = 1st | location = Berkeley, CA | isbn = 978-0-9630096-9-2 | oclc = 38503252 | chapter-url = https://www.erowid.org/library/books_online/tihkal/tihkal43.shtml | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=jl_ik66IumUC | quote = (with 4 mgs, smoking) "This was the free base. I remember the pipe, and the inhalation and, with the pouring of a small glass of scotch, I settled down in front of the TV to watch a re-run of Star Trek. That was it. I came to some time later in the front room of a professional ally of mine, who had by chance discovered me walking down the street near his house. I do not recall, nor have I been able to regain any memories of the time I was 'out there.' I apparently experienced no physical discomfort from the drug. In fact I distinctly remember feeling very comfortable when I awoke. Clearly this compound is some weird-ass shit."}}</ref> The chemist publicly shared further details of the incident during an interview with psychedelic journalist [[Hamilton Morris]] in 2021, describing it as a cautionary tale of the risks of self-experimentation with little-known psychoactive drugs and the importance of careful dose escalation and of having a trip sitter.<ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" />

After leaving the Nichols lab, Oberlender worked as an [[assistant professor]] of medicinal chemistry at the [[University of the Pacific (United States)|University of the Pacific]] in [[Stockton, California]].<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> In 2000, he joined New River Pharmaceuticals in [[Blacksburg, Virginia]] and served as a director of [[drug misuse]] science.<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> While at New River Pharmaceuticals, Oberlender had a key role in discovering and developing the misuse-resistant [[dextroamphetamine]] [[prodrug]] and psychostimulant [[lisdexamfetamine]], which had the developmental code name ''NRP-104''.<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" /><ref name="MorrisOberlender2021" /> Oberlender and colleagues [[patent]]ed lisdexamfetamine in 2006 and 2007.<ref name="US7105486B2">Mickle, T., Krishnan, S., Bishop, B., Lauderback, C., Moncrief, J. S., Oberlender, R., & Piccariello, T. (2006). Abuse‐resistant amphetamine compounds (US 7,105,486 B2). United States. https://patents.google.com/patent/US7105486B2/en</ref><ref name="US20070042955">Mickle, T., Krishnan, S., Bishop, B., Lauderback, C., Moncrief, J. S., Oberlender, R., ... & Verbicky, C. A. (2007). Abuse-resistant amphetamine prodrugs. US20070042955 (A1), 111. https://patents.google.com/patent/US20070042955A1/</ref> New River Pharmaceuticals was purchased by [[Shire (pharmaceutical company)|Shire]] in 2007.<ref name="PharmaTimes2007">{{cite web | title=Shire buys New River Pharmaceuticals for $2.6 billion | website=PharmaTimes | date=21 February 2007 | url=https://pharmatimes.com/news/shire_buys_new_river_pharmaceuticals_for_2-6_billion_989405/ | access-date=16 June 2025}}</ref> That same year, lisdexamfetamine was initially approved and introduced for medical use under the brand name Vyvanse in the [[United States]].<ref name="PharmaTimes2007" /><ref name="AdisInsight">{{cite web | title=Lisdexamfetamine | website=AdisInsight | date=5 November 2023 | url=https://adisinsight.springer.com/drugs/800020876 | access-date=16 June 2025}}</ref> Following these events, Oberlender started working at Synthonics in Blackburg, Virginia and began developing metal-coordinated pharmaceutical drugs at the company.<ref name="MichaelJFoxFoundation" />
